reasoning: Lack of knowledge does not simply erase responsibility in these rules. Their specified remedies should not automatically be generalized to every deliberate offense.
scope: This describes the law’s framing, not a modern judgment of culpability, evidence of uniform enforcement or a comprehensive theory of forgiveness.

title: The required offering changes with what a person can afford
summary: A person unable to afford a flock animal may bring birds, or ultimately flour.
text: Chapter 5 gives a flock animal, two birds if that is unaffordable, and flour if the birds are also unaffordable. The flour sin offering specifically omits oil and frankincense. Leviticus 12 permits two birds instead of the standard childbirth offering when a lamb is unaffordable. Leviticus 14 gives a reduced cleansing offering for poverty, but still requires one lamb. These distinct allowances do not support substituting flour in every case.
reasoning: The alternatives are explicit exceptions to the standard requirement, including a non-animal offering in this case. The no-oil rule also distinguishes it from the grain offering of chapter 2.
scope: These allowances apply to the cases under discussion; they do not prove that every sacrificial obligation allowed the same substitutes or quantify ancient household wealth.

title: A ritual offering does not replace restitution
summary: Restoration of property, an additional fifth and an offering appear together.
text: Harm to sacred property requires compensation plus a fifth. Deceit over entrusted, stolen or found property likewise requires restoration to its owner with an added fifth, alongside a ram offering. Leviticus 22:14 also requires replacement plus a fifth when sacred food is eaten unwittingly.
reasoning: The stated remedy combines material repair with ritual atonement. It should not be summarized as forgiveness obtained merely by presenting an animal.
scope: This describes these particular cases. It does not resolve every restitution rule in other law collections or demonstrate historical collection and enforcement.

title: Fire marks acceptance and then judgment
summary: Consecutive scenes assign opposite outcomes to fire described as coming from God.
text: At the inauguration, fire consumes the altar offering and the people respond with awe. In the next scene, Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire and die when fire comes from God.
reasoning: The narrative contrasts authorized worship with an unauthorized act. It gives no detailed physical account of either fire event.
scope: The account identifies the act as uncommanded, but does not fully specify the procedural breach, independently verify the deaths or establish a natural mechanism.

title: The wine prohibition does not prove the brothers were intoxicated
summary: The later rule concerns priests entering the sanctuary and performing their duties.
text: After Nadab and Abihu’s deaths, Aaron is told that he and his sons must not drink wine or strong drink when entering the sanctuary. Distinguishing sacred categories and teaching are stated purposes.
reasoning: The placement may invite a connection with the preceding episode, but the account never explicitly says the brothers drank. That diagnosis would be an inference.
scope: This establishes the rule’s stated setting, not a ban on every person drinking in every circumstance or proof of the brothers’ condition.

title: An edible animal’s carcass can still transmit ritual uncleanness
summary: Permission to eat an animal category does not make every contact with its dead body clean.
text: The law distinguishes allowed animal categories, contact with carcasses, washing and waiting until evening. It explicitly includes carcasses of animals otherwise permitted for food and gives exceptions for water sources and dry seed.
reasoning: Food classification and contact rules address different circumstances. The exceptions also prevent treating every contact as one identical rule.
scope: The passage states holiness as its rationale. Historical health effects, pathogen transmission and the zoological descriptions in verses 4–23 require separate evidence.

title: The purification periods differ by the child’s sex
summary: The prescribed periods total forty days after a son and eighty after a daughter.
text: The law gives seven days followed by thirty-three after a son, and fourteen followed by sixty-six after a daughter. It specifies sanctuary restrictions and a concluding offering, with an affordability allowance.
reasoning: Both components double in the second case. The text states the difference but provides no biological explanation for it.
scope: This identifies an unequal ritual prescription. It cannot establish that biological recovery takes twice as long after a daughter, explain the historical rationale or settle its ethical evaluation.

title: The KJV leprosy category extends beyond modern Hansen’s disease
summary: The same translated category is applied to skin, fabrics and houses.
text: Leviticus examines skin changes, including conditions declared clean, then applies leprosy language to fabric and house surfaces. Modern Hansen’s disease is a specific bacterial disease; CDC describes clinical diagnosis and confirmation using skin or nerve biopsy and staining.
reasoning: Applying the biblical category to materials as well as people shows that it cannot simply identify one modern human disease in every occurrence. Similar English names do not establish identical diagnostic criteria.
scope: This comparison does not diagnose any ancient individual, identify every skin condition or determine which organism affected a garment or house. Modern disease causation does not resolve all translation questions.

sources.label: CDC · clinical overview of Hansen’s disease

title: The cleansing ceremony follows a finding of healing
summary: The priest first finds the condition healed, then begins the bird and washing ceremony.
text: Verse 3 places healing before the instructions for birds, blood, washing, shaving and later offerings. The person’s return also occurs in stages.
reasoning: The sequence does not present the bird ceremony as the action that first cures the skin condition. Ritual restoration and a claim of medical treatment should not be conflated.
scope: The account does not explain what caused recovery, measure treatment efficacy or establish the health effects of each ritual action.

title: Ordinary and prolonged discharges have different procedures
summary: The law distinguishes temporary uncleanness after semen discharge from longer discharge-related procedures.
text: Semen discharge and intercourse require washing and waiting until evening. Menstruation, prolonged bleeding and other discharges have different periods and, in specified cases, offerings. The concluding rationale concerns protecting the sanctuary.
reasoning: The text assigns ritual status to several bodily conditions. It does not say that every one of these conditions is a moral offense or that every discharge has the same cause.
scope: This is a reading of the stated categories, not a modern diagnosis or evidence that every condition is contagious. Medical identification and historical interpretation require additional research.

title: The two goats have distinct roles
summary: One goat is killed for the offering; the other is sent alive into the wilderness.
text: Lots distinguish the goats. One supplies sacrificial blood, while the live goat receives the confession and is led away. The KJV chapter’s footnote identifies Azazel behind its scapegoat wording.
reasoning: The two actions belong to different animals within one procedure. The passage explicitly instructs release of the live goat; it does not describe killing both.
scope: This identifies the stated ritual sequence. The meaning of Azazel, comparative ritual history and later practices require further research; the text alone does not establish a physical mechanism of removing guilt.

title: Entry behind the veil is restricted and procedural
summary: The high-priestly rite uses linen clothing, incense and blood, with others excluded during the entry.
text: The chapter follows the deaths of Aaron’s sons, forbids unrestricted entry and specifies preparations. It assigns the rite to a particular annual date and the succession of the anointed priest.
reasoning: A priest’s ordinary service and this restricted entry are different settings. The prescribed clothing and exclusion rules need to be read with that special procedure.
scope: The law’s schedule and stated danger do not independently show historical observance, explain a biological cause of death or reconstruct all later temple practice.

title: Blood’s biological role and its ritual role are different claims
summary: The passage connects blood with life and altar atonement while forbidding its consumption.
text: Leviticus gives a religious rationale for reserving blood and directs hunters to pour it out. Modern physiology describes blood circulating oxygen through the heart, lungs and body.
reasoning: Blood’s role in sustaining the body is compatible with a broad association between blood and life. That biological function does not experimentally establish the separate claim about atonement.
scope: The comparison does not show that the passage explains modern circulation, equate life solely with blood or infer a universal food-safety rule. The religious claim requires its own interpretive framework.

sources.label: NHLBI, NIH · blood flow and oxygen circulation

title: A brother’s wife prohibition and a conditional marriage duty
summary: Leviticus prohibits relations with a brother’s wife; Deuteronomy requires marriage in a specified widowhood case.
text: Deuteronomy describes brothers dwelling together, one dying without a child, and a surviving brother’s duty to marry the widow to preserve the dead brother’s name. It also gives a public procedure for refusal. Leviticus 20:21 repeats the brother’s-wife prohibition with a childlessness sanction. This differs from the prior childlessness of the deceased brother that triggers Deuteronomy’s widowhood procedure.
reasoning: The conditions support reading the widowhood duty as a limited exception to the kinship prohibition. Leviticus 18:16 does not spell out that exception, so the relationship between these laws still needs interpretation.
scope: This identifies the textual tension and a possible contextual reading. It does not prove uniform historical practice, settle later legal applications or justify the arrangement by present-day standards.

title: Support for the poor accompanies impartial judgment
summary: Harvest provisions for poor people and residents coexist with a ban on favoring rich or poor in judgment.
text: The chapter reserves gleanings, requires prompt wages, forbids abusing deaf or blind people, commands love for the resident stranger and requires honest measures. Its judicial rule forbids favoritism based on either poverty or power.
reasoning: Material assistance and deciding a legal case are different activities. Requiring support for vulnerable people does not here require a judge to decide solely according to someone’s economic status.
scope: This describes the stated duties. Actual enforcement, the social reach of resident status and broader unequal legal statuses require historical and comparative research.

title: The collection prescribes several kinds of sanctions
summary: Death, being cut off and childlessness are described separately rather than as one uniform penalty.
text: The chapter prescribes death for specified offenses, including adultery and the male same-sex act it prohibits. Other kinship offenses receive language about being cut off, bearing iniquity or childlessness.
reasoning: The wording distinguishes sanctions. The meaning and administration of being cut off cannot simply be assumed identical to every explicit execution command.
scope: This records the ancient prescriptions without endorsing them. It does not establish actual enforcement or a biological cause of childlessness; historical interpretation and ethical evaluation remain separate tasks.

title: Priests and the high priest have different rules for the dead
summary: Ordinary priests have named family exceptions; the high priest’s rule excludes even parents.
text: The opening permits a priest’s contact-related defilement for certain close relatives. The later section explicitly addresses the high priest and forbids it even for father or mother, alongside mourning and sanctuary restrictions.
reasoning: The change in the addressed office explains why the permissions differ. Reading both sections as rules for one undifferentiated priestly role misses that distinction.
scope: The text describes office-specific restrictions. It does not document how every burial or bereavement was handled historically or settle the human consequences of these requirements.

title: Restrictions on altar service and sacred food are distinct
summary: A descendant of Aaron with a listed bodily condition may eat sacred food while barred from altar service.
text: Chapter 21 excludes those with listed bodily conditions from specified sanctuary duties but expressly permits sacred food. Chapter 22 separately prohibits eating while ritually unclean and gives conditions for resuming it.
reasoning: Service eligibility and temporary purity status are different criteria. Permission to eat under the first rule does not cancel the second rule’s conditions.
scope: These are restrictive ancient ritual categories, not proof that disability entails moral wrongdoing. Their origins, social effects and ethics need additional research; the record does not endorse exclusion today.

title: A freewill-offering exception qualifies the animal rules
summary: A stated exception for certain bodily irregularities differs between freewill offerings and vows.
text: After general requirements for animals without blemish, verse 23 permits a bullock or lamb with a part described as superfluous or lacking for a freewill offering, but not for a vow. Other specified injuries remain prohibited.
reasoning: The text supplies a limited exception tied to offering type. It should not be expanded into permission for every listed defect in every offering.
scope: This compares the wording and exception. Exact anatomical terminology, textual variants and later legal classifications remain to be researched.

title: Thanksgiving and vow offerings have different eating deadlines
summary: Thanksgiving meat has a same-day deadline; the vow or voluntary offering rule permits the following day.
text: Chapter 7 distinguishes thanksgiving from vow or voluntary peace offerings. Chapter 22 repeats the same-day thanksgiving rule. Chapter 19 gives a two-day peace-offering rule without naming thanksgiving there.
reasoning: The category distinction in chapter 7 offers context for the different deadlines. The broad wording of chapter 19 still requires interpretation rather than treating every peace offering as automatically identical.
scope: This concerns ritual timing. The passages do not supply a universal microbiological shelf-life or quantify food-safety effects, and wider legal history remains open.
